speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform hon. members that the Canadian wheat board is announcing in Winnipeg today that it has negotiated a contract for the sale of approximately 500,000 metric tons of wheat for shipment to Czechoslovakia. This sale, totalling approximately 18.4 million bushels, is for shipment during the period August to November, 1964.
This is the second sale made to Czechoslovakia under the provisions of the long term agreement signed on October 29, 1963. Of the 500,000 metric tons purchased, 230,000 tons represent the completion of the quantity that Czechoslovakia had agreed to buy during the first year of the agreement, and the balance of 270,000 tons applies against the second agreement year which commences October 30, 1964.
Payment for the wheat is to be made on the basis of 10 per cent at time of shipment with the balance to be paid in equal instalments, plus interest, at two, two and a half and three years respectively. These credit arrangements were authorized by the government of Canada under the provisions of the Export Credits Insurance Act.

On the orders of the day:

I have a question for the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In his absence perhaps I may direct it to the acting minister or the Minister of Agriculture. It relates to the grain sale which was announced today by the Minister of Agriculture. Could the house be informed whether it was made clear to those negotiating on behalf of Czechoslovakia what financial benefits could accrue both to Czechoslovakia and to western farmers by agreeing to the shipment of a considerable amount of this grain through the port of Churchill? If this was not made
clear to them, will the minister assure the house that it will be made clear to them in future.

request to the chairman of the wheat board. [Translation]

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN INTERNATIONAL SATELLITE SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Acting Prime Minister in connection with the international satellite communication system. What was the basis upon which Canada decided to make a contribution to this system; and is the minister in a position to give the reason why the

Inquiries of the Ministry United States defence department has withdrawn from the satellite communication consortia and what the effects of the withdrawal of the United States will be on probable costs?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN INTERNATIONAL SATELLITE SYSTEMS
speechtext: I will ask the Minister of Transport to answer that question.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN INTERNATIONAL SATELLITE SYSTEMS
speechtext: I should not like, Mr. Speaker, to make a statement without very careful reference to the documents, but my impression is that it was not a sudden or precipitate withdrawal. The way in which the satellite communication system is being worked out is that it would provide for participation by any countries which wished to participate. I think hon. members will quickly appreciate that this might have certain consequences from the point of view of certain types of military communications. I do not think it was contemplated that even though the defence services of the United States or any other country did not participate directly in the satellite system itself, that would not mean that certain types of communications would not use that system in exactly the same way as the defence forces now use other communication systems than their own.

subtopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN INTERNATIONAL SATELLITE SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister has said it was not precipitate action on the part of the United States. However, the New York Times report indicates that this is another reversal of the Pentagon's on again-off again efforts in the development of a military communications satellite system.
I realize that it is difficult for the minister to answer without having the material before him, but I should like the minister to give the house a full answer in this regard and also to indicate what the expenditures will be on the part of Canada in this connection, as well as the reason Canada should be assuming a major responsibility in so far as the expenditure is concerned in this connection at a time when the United States, which is so necessarily interested in matters such as this, is withdrawing.

subtopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN INTERNATIONAL SATELLITE SYSTEMS
speechtext:
In the first place, sir, I do not think it would be appropriate for me, with or without notice, to comment on the policies of the government of the United States. We are answerable in parliament for what we do and not for what other countries do. The only aspect of United States policy that would be of concern to us would be if the United States government decided not to participate in this system. Which agency of

the United States government may participate is surely a matter for the United States.
I have no information that the United States government, which has a chosen agency which is partially privately owned and partially publicly owned, does not intend to participate as a major partner in this project. I am quite sure if there was any decision that the United States was not participating in that way, there would be no project at all and, therefore, there would be no problem of Canada's participation.
Assuming there has been no change so far as the United States government is concerned-I feel quite sure I would have heard about it more directly than through the New York Times if there had been-and assuming that negotiations are going to go on in Washington on the basis on which I understood they were going on, which involved no participation by the United States defence department at all, then the reason Canada is participating to the extent it is is that we believe this is a venture of great importance in the communications field. This was true of the telephone cable project in which we participated some years ago. We feel this is going to be a very important means of communication, and a profitable means of communication over a long period. Hon. members will have noted only yesterday the report of the C.O.T.C. which was gratifying in that it showed a large profit was being made on their operations.
Now, it is thought there is a very distinct probability that satellite communications will supplement to a very great extent cable telephonic communications, and that this, to a great degree at any rate, is the wave of the future in communications. We felt it was desirable that Canada should participate, for exactly the same reasons we are participating in the telephonic cables, and should have a sufficiently large interest in it to have a permanent say in its direction. We feel this will be the kind of investment that will pay dividends, and I do not mean just dividends in good will or anything of that sort but cash dividends in due course to the investors.

subtopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN INTERNATIONAL SATELLITE SYSTEMS
speechtext: I thank the minister for his explanation. Of course everybody is in agreement that Canada should participate in intercommunications. When we were in office we participated in the commonwealth telephone system, so it is not anything new. It was during our administration that it was started.

subtopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN INTERNATIONAL SATELLITE SYSTEMS
speechtext: I am sure the right hon. gentleman does not want to misrepresent the facts. It was started by the St. Laurent government when I was a member of that government.

subtopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN INTERNATIONAL SATELLITE SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, they started a lot of things but did not go ahead, and this was one of those. Just a moment ago I was going to compliment the minister on the very good answer he gave, but now he has spoiled it all.
Does he say the United States defence department did not notify Canada as to its attitude in this regard? I must say I am surprised if there has been no communication.

subtopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN INTERNATIONAL SATELLITE SYSTEMS
speechtext:
I said no such thing at all. I said it was my understanding even before we went to this conference that the United States defence department was not going to be participating in it. I believe that will be found to be the fact; but I think it is very wrong for members of the Canadian government to be interpreting the policies of the United States and the administration of the United States.
Since the right hon. gentleman has introduced the irrelevancy might I point out I was present at the cable laying at Clarenville, Newfoundland, as the representative of the government of Canada, and that was before the right hon. gentleman even became the leader of his party.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of personal priv-

5S41
ilege. I have been reliably informed, and have no reason to doubt, that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, either on his own initiative or on the initiative of a member of his staff, has had printed and framed at public expense for hanging in one or both of his offices-because two copies were framed-one sentence of a speech I made in this house on June 22 as reported at page 4564 of Hansard, when I said:
I like the type of man who will try to get into this country illegally.
While I have tried to keep under control any feelings I might have of pride and satisfaction at having words of mine grace the walls of the minister's office and publicized in this manner, I would like to think the minister would make sure that visitors to his office were supplied with copies of the full text of my speech. Thus the sentence to which the minister attaches such significance and has chosen to immortalize may be interpreted in its true light and with a sense of fair proportion.
May I, when I state this question of privilege, remind the house that in the early days of this country, before immigration procedures became formalized, many of our ancestors found haven and refuge here because of their daring and initiative. Then in a later period of our history I recall the Estonian refugees who landed in Saint John, New Brunswick, in the late 1940's after a hazardous journey across the north Atlantic in a sailboat. There are many such examples of courage and daring which were technically illegal but Canada, I submit, is a better place because these people are here. Also, Mr. Speaker, I have been reminded that the modern state of Israel owes a large portion of its population to such methods, and is proud of the fact.
I will be glad to arrange to send an adequate and generous supply of copies of my speech to the minister if he thinks it inappropriate to charge the public purse with copies for his own use.

Mr. Speaker, last Tuesday the hon. member for Chapleau (Mr. Laprise) asked me whether any action had been taken in order to reimburse for their moving expenses the families which have been forced to move on account of the closing of the radar station at Parent.
In answer I may tell him that there were 66 full time employees at the Parent air base at the time of its closing. Fifty two of them have now got other employment.
The Department of National Defence has secured from the treasury board a special authorization to reimburse the moving expenses up to $500 in the case of every surplus employee transferred to a position in the federal government somewhere else. However, this special authorization is restricted to employees coming under the Civil Service Act and who occupy a post above the normal admission level. Experience shows that most surplus employees who accept transfers involving a change of residence can take advantage of this special authorization.
In the case of Parent, three surplus employees were provided assistance for their moving costs.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
Last night in the confusion and perhaps because of my inadequate knowledge of the standing orders, I thought I had to resume my seat at six o'clock, but someone else called it six o'clock, which I should have done myself.
I thank you for your fairness toward me, because I have something else to say before concluding my remarks on Bill No. C-110.
It must be realized that two very important and obvious points emerge from this bill. There is, first of all, the assistance to be given to students and, second, the granting of this aid with respect to the constitution.
All hon. members admit that our students need some assistance at the present time to pay their tuition fees. There is no doubt about that. It is admitted that they absolutely need some assistance. We have proof of this every day in the letters and telegrams from our constituents, asking us to pass legislation providing for some assistance to students throughout Canada.
On the other hand, this assistance must not be a burden. When we are anxious to help someone, we do it gratuitously. We do not put him under a yoke, as I said yesterday.
Loans to Students
If, in order to help someone, we must dedicate him, so to speak, to the service of the banks for ten, 15 or 20 years of his life, I maintain that we are helping him the wrong way. If, for instance, a man buys his son a car, knowing his son cannot drive, and he buys him one anyway and his son goes over a cliff, I feel that this father has acted foolishly and irresponsibly.
That is how the federal government intends to help students, by putting a rope around their necks.
My second point concerns respect for the constitution. If we must indeed help, we must do it within the constitution. All members of this house know that education comes exclusively under the jurisdiction of the provinces and that this is guaranteed by the constitution.
Yesterday I heard an hon. member claim that the rights of the province of Quebec were safeguarded, but I wonder to what degree, when the interests are to be paid by the federal government. The students are referred to the chartered banks, and if they agree to lend them money, the government guarantees to the chartered banks payment of interest for five years.
Now, I do not understand how the Liberal members can claim that the rights of the province of Quebec are safeguarded simply because the federal government pays the interest to the banks. It is precisely on this point that we object. Whether it is given directly or indirectly, the money is given anyway, and it will come out of the taxes levied in the province of Quebec. That is where we say that the federal government, through this legislation, is encroaching on the rights of the province of Quebec, as well as on the rights of the other provinces.
That is why, generally speaking, Mr. Speaker, we, in the Social Credit rally, want to introduce an amendment which will permit the government to respect the constitution and guarantee to the students the amounts of money they require to complete their education.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Plourde):
That the Bill C-110 be not now read a second time, but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should consider the opportunity to present new legislation which would authorize the Bank of Canada to supply to the provinces the necessary credits to permit them to fulfil completely their responsibilities in the field of education.

It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy, or provisions of the bill, or expressing opinions as to any circumstances connected with its introduction, or prosecution-

Mr. Speaker, I feel it is my duty to take part in this debate as a representative from a region where is located the most flourishing university of the country and on the border of which is located a university recognized throughout Canada, that is the universities of Sherbrooke, and Bishop's at Lennoxville.
Another reason why I wish to speak on this issue is that I live in a province which is undergoing deep changes in all fields, but especially as far as education is concerned.
I should like to say that I am in favour of any form of assistance to students, even if that system should run students into debt, as the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) pointed out, because I feel it is better to be in debt at the end of one's studies than not to complete those studies.
I know what that means personally, because I had to get into debt to finish my studies. As everybody knows, that is a painful situation and it may be that the student who has to work because of his financial troubles will not benefit from his studies as much as he should. Our students must not, on account of a lack of funds, be placed in the situation where they will one day have to admit that they are not as competent as they would have been if they had had no worry besides their studies.
Even though it is incomplete and unconstitutional, as I will show later on, the proposal under consideration is worth while, and the government was well-intentioned in introducing this legislation.
As I said, I believe the bill is definitely incomplete, and particularly unconstitutional. I should like to go over it, step by step, starting with section 2 giving the definition of "bank":

"bank" means a bank to which the Bank Act applies.
Now, under the Bank Act, the caisses populaires will not be allowed to make loans to students under this legislation. Failure to authorize the caisses populaires to act as lending institutions under this act is a slight on the province of Quebec, for there are more than 1,300 branches of caisses populaires in the province of Quebec, all sound institutions which can, just as well as the banks, comply with the requirements of this bill.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, here is how section 2(e) defines "certificate of eligibility":
-a certificate in prescribed form issued or caused to be issued by an appropriate authority relating to a qualifying student-
I read the whole bill and I failed to find what is a "qualifying student", what are the requirements asked of a student to become eligible for those loans.
I think there should be a definition stipulating that any student who passes his examinations is eligible to apply for a loan. I think that should have been specified in the bill.
The bill provides that only full time university students may benefit from those loans.
There are in my riding, as in all university towns, a growing number of adults who wish to get a university education by taking evening courses, or who would like to go back for a year in order to get enough credits to obtain a B.A. or some other diploma they could show the boss and thereby get a promotion.
I feel it was a great mistake, in this bill, not to have adults also entitled to those loans so they could improve their education.
Now, there is another point I think was overlooked in the determination of the required qualifications to obtain such a loan.
I refer to a student who spends two years in the same grade. Under this legislation, would he be eligible for the same loan the second year? Must the amount of $5,000 be spread over five consecutive successful years in university, or will the student who has failed one year still be entitled to the loan for that year?
Nothing in the bill covers the case where a student, after completing his university studies and obtained the amount of $5,000, should decide to specialize. Will he have to pay back his loan immediately, that is, after a six-month period, when he may still find himself taking courses following a five year period, according to the requirements of his studies, his specialty or doctorate?

In my opinion, this point should have been set out clearly in the bill.
Clause 9 also provides that:
The minister may pay to a bank a prescribed amount in respect of any sum collected by a bank on behalf of Her Majesty from a borrower after any payment is made by the minister to that bank pursuant to section 7. in respect of a guaranteed student loan made to that borrower.
I think that the amount in question should have been specified in this clause, and if the amounts claimed by the banks are too high and the government has to pay an unreasonable amount for the collection thereof, I feel that this will increase the rate of interest on each loan.
Now that I have raised some points and mentioned some deficiencies in this bill, I should like to deal with the constitutional part thereof.
I do not want to speak of federal intrusion in a provincial field because many others have dealt with that matter. As far as I am concerned, I do not think that the fact that student loans are provided by the federal government constitutes an intrusion in provincial affairs. In my opinion, this is strictly a business proposition and students are free to borrow or not to borrow the money, according to their own convictions. Besides, the sums to be borrowed under this legislation will not necessarily be used entirely to pay for their studies. The borrower is free to use his money as he sees fit.
I do not think that it is any intrusion in the field of education to offer money to someone with the idea that, later on the amount will be used to complete his studies, because the student can use the money for all sorts of things. In my opinion, this is purely and simply a business proposition.
But the constitutional aspect that I want to raise concerns section 15 of the bill, which says:
A guaranteed student loan made by a bank to a borrower not of full age, and interest thereon other than interest payable under section 6, is recoverable by a bank from the borrower as though the borrower had been of full age at the time the loan was made.
The point is, Mr. Speaker, that in the province of Quebec we have a civil code. We are governed by it and the legal capacity of people is determined by the civil code of the province of Quebec, while in the other provinces, the legal capacity is determined by the common law.
Under section 986 of the civil code of the province of Quebec, we see that:

Those legally incapable of contracting are:
Minors, in the cases and according to the provisions contained in this code;
Then there is a list of other persons unable to enter into contracts.
Cases where minors can enter into contracts are listed in the following section which gives exceptions and details. Section 1005 states the following:
A minor who is a banker, trader or mechanic is not relievable for cause of lesion from contracts made for the purposes of his business or trade.
There is no mention of students in that section since it mentions only bankers, traders or mechanics. Consequently, the minors in question, under that act, are neither bankers, traders nor mechanics.
There is also section 1011 which could alleviate suspicions. It says that the money paid during the minority cannot be exacted, unless it is proved that what has been so paid has turned to their profit.
This section might justify section 15 of the bill, but I think that this case does not apply either, because this section provides mostly for the cases where under age students involved sell or buy something for a price and try to obtain repayment of the money they would have paid, when they would come of age or even before when they were unable to enter into a contract.
Even though this section could remove in the minister's mind the suspicions that the government certainly has about those loans- because if it had no suspicions with regard to minors, this section would have been unnecessary-even though this section could lead them to believe it would be legal, I think that the fact alone that the federal government attempts to legislate on the legal capacity of the Quebec people makes the whole measure, and not only section 15, unconstitutional.
Consequently, section 15 proposes an amendment to the civil code of the province of Quebec, that only the Quebec legislature is entitled to make under the constitution.
If we allow this bill to be passed in this house, it will be a dangerous precedent, because then, it will be possible federal legislation, to amend the civil code of the province of Quebec and to insert in it sections such as section 15 of the present bill.

Mr. Speaker, the matter I am now discussing is simply the legality of section 15 of this bill.
I think that common law is constituted by federal and provincial legislation passed by the other provinces, except Quebec, and if this section is accepted by Quebec, it is also accepted by the other provinces, because they are governed by common law. In the province of Quebec, it is different. In fact, we are not governed by common law, but we have our own laws, our civil code. Therefore, we cannot accept to have this section included in legislation which could, in future, be accepted in the province of Quebec.
In my opinion, the only legal and constitutional way to draw up such a clause would be to add the following at the end: As if the latter had been of age at the time the loan was granted, except in the province of Quebec where the legal capacity of citizens is determined by the civil code of the province of Quebec.

Then, if the province of Quebec wishes to establish its own system of loans to students, it could legislate and amend the civil code by stipulating in its bill: For the purposes of loans to students in the province of Quebec, those under age will be considered as being of age at the time of the loan.
But at the present time, a federal piece of legislation changes the legal capacity of those under age in Quebec and I feel that it is entirely unconstitutional and that the principle is unacceptable to the citizens of Quebec.
Those are, Mr. Speaker, the few remarks which I wanted to make about the bill under consideration. Before moving passage of this bill, I believe that the Minister of Finance, in consultation with the Minister of Justice, should find another formula to amend that clause. He should ask the advice of experts or others. In any case, the present provisions of section 15 are unacceptable and I do not think that a single Quebec citizen could vote in favour of that clause, because it would be to vote in favour of a very dangerous precedent.
Even in the good faith of students or of those covered by that bill can be accepted beforehand, I feel that we cannot, on that matter of principle, support such a bill, because it affects directly what, to my mind, is the most sacred right of the Quebec citizens, the right to draw up their own civil legislation.

I am pleased to be able to participate in this debate today and speak in support of the student loans bill for post-secondary school students. I wish to take a few minutes of the time of the house to make a suggestion which I hope the government will take into consideration in the near future. I am sure most members are aware that at the present time the armed services recruit people in their last years of higher education, then pay for their final years of schooling. In return the students serve either three, four or five years in the armed services.
I should like to suggest to the government that they consider this method of repayment of the loan instead of cash. We could possibly call it a time repayment. The recipient of the student loan would donate, if you want to use that word, his services for a period of time in his chosen profession to the government of Canada. This time would be in proportion to the investment that Canada had made in his career. During his period of serv-
Loans to Students
ice he could be sent anywhere overseas-I am thinking particularly of the backward countries of Asia and Africa-where his ability, skills and training would help others to help themselves. It would be the primary occupation of this person to teach these backward people so that they in turn could pass on this information-to others of their own race and their own land.
In this way, Mr. Speaker, we could help the underdeveloped and poorly educated peoples to progress with their own educational systems. This would then become part of Canada's external aid program. Canada would be doing this as part of a long range aid program to these countries, and at the same time would benefit her own Canadian citizens by providing them with needed help for their education via this student loans measure.
Once the person had served his time, whatever time was decided upon, he would then be free to undertake any employment he wished in any place. It is a well known fact, Mr. Speaker, that many of our Canadian people who are highly trained and educated migrate to the United States. This is one export, that of Canadian skills and brains, that we should endeavour to decrease. I feel the system I have suggested would encourage Canadians, after this period of service was up, to remain in this country and use their skills and their knowledge for the benefit of Canadians as a whole. If thought desirable, a further clause could be added to the bill requiring Canadian residence for a specific period of time as a condition of the granting of such loan.
So far as the amendment is concerned and the feeling of some members that this is unconstitutional, I am not a constitutional expert but I should like to point out that this bill does not create a precedent in the matter of federal aid for education. I would point members to the fact that after world war II thousands of veterans received their education under the auspices of the Department of Veterans Affairs. That department paid their fees, gave them a book allowance, and paid them a monthly allowance while they attended university. Many thousands of veterans used this federal aid to obtain their education and are now using their skills and their training to the benefit of Canada and Canadians. Without this aid that was provided by the federal government, many of these students would not have had the opportunity to continue their studies.
I promised the house I would only take a few minutes of its time, Mr. Speaker. In sum-

mary I would just like to say that the suggestion I have made to the government that the money be repaid by donating their time, in lieu of money, to Canada's external aid program would benefit many different people and many different areas. Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity to say a few words on this legislation, and like the hon. member who has just sat down I am utterly sincere when I say "a few words." I was impressed with his suggestion and I think it should receive favourable consideration.
I am going to be brief because essentially I agree with this legislation. Sometimes it is said that parliamentarians take an awful long time to say yes, but that is the essence of the parliamentary system. As I say, I am going to be brief because I am one of those who believe the House of Commons should not be sitting in July and August. If we have come to the stage that it takes the House of Commons ten months to transact the people's business, all I can say is that I have never been able to see anything sacrosanct about the months of July and August and why these should be included among those ten months devoted to our work in Ottawa. Also, since we are talking about youth it would be a good thing to allow some of us young if not young looking members to spend some time with the members of our families, and it is not easy to do that labouring in heat oppressed Ottawa.
I shall not, like some members, give a catalogue of universities. Much of my life has been spent in universities. I recall a former professor who used to say in high dudgeon when he was dissatisfied with administration policy, "I have been kicked out of better universities than this." I have never had that actually happen to me, but over the years I have come to know something about the tremendous needs of universities and I do have the honour to represent a constituency which has two fine educational institutions whose problems are similar, if not identical, to those facing every institution of higher learning in the country. St. Dunstan's University is an institution which for over a century has
[Mr. Harley.l
served the whole of Prince Edward Island, with students coming to it from beyond the province and indeed beyond the country. Prince of Wales college is a junior college maintained by the provincial government.
I am in agreement with those who have said heretofore that while this is important it is not sufficient, and in my opinion it is not so important as some of the other youth plans of the government. The youth plans which the Liberal party had when it was seeking to be the government were certainly impressive, and if I may give the government a bit of political advice-and I should not do this as a member of the opposition-one of the problems it is facing today is that our young people are becoming a bit disillusioned and disturbed by the non-fulfilment of some of the government's promises. The scholarship plan was an important one.
It has already been laid on the record and the story well told that universities today face great problems in the provision of buildings and facilities. I would not say that there were not some potential university students in the country who cannot finance their education, but I think all educators know this problem is not nearly as grievous as it once was. I would not suggest either that it is a good thing for young people to struggle and strive to take on all sorts of extra moonlighting jobs in order to complete their university training. Perhaps for a Calvinist I am a little weak-kneed in stating this point, but even though I did do it myself I would not prescribe it as a recipe for all aspiring students. Therefore I commend the government for what has been done. But the government must do more.
We have been talking about priority legislation. Sometimes we wonder whether this is more important than that, whether something is so important that we must do it before we can have an adjournment, and whether something else may be delayed. Let us not delude ourselves. There is nothing as important as the very subject with which we are coping today. Someone has said that references to the future of our country and its human potential are cliches. Of course they are but none the less true. We may want vast public works; we may want a lot of things, but if we do not have a highly trained group of young people to cope with the complexities of modern life in this highly advanced country, then we will have failed.
I know there are problems of jurisdiction. I know that education is, if I may say so, the sacred right of the provinces. I know too

that in education, as in many other problems, the resources of some of our provinces are not sufficient to meet the needs. So what do we do under those circumstances?
In a publication which recently came to me, "Financing Higher Education in Canada" published by the Canadian universities foundation, I note that in the years 1958 to 1963 federal government support to universities totalled $245 million. We cannot say that the federal government is not involved in education. Many examples of this have been cited. Nor can we ever expect this country, composed as it is of provinces of such varying resources, so unequal in wealth, will ever see a situation where the demands upon the federal government through whatever agencies may be involved will not become greater and greater rather than diminish.
This is not the place to enter into the kind of argument which the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman) made yesterday, although I believe it is a tremendously important field to which Canadians, and certainly Canadian legislators, must soon direct themselves. As a great Canadian scholar said the other day, so often we find that those in the dominion field of government approach the provinces with such timorous politeness, and it seems that very little is left on the dominion side of things.
As I was thinking of the importance of this subject, Mr. Speaker, hoping that I might join my voice with those of my colleagues who have supported the government, and not ignoring the very valid criticisms which have come from all parties in the house, my mind went back to a very important little story that I read some time ago about that wonderful part of the United States, Vermont, which, at its best, is very much like the maritime provinces. Dorothy Canfield Fisher in her book the "Vermont Tradition" tells a story which strikes me as being most germane to our discussion. In her home town there was a great problem about highways and an urgently pressing problem about a bridge, and in mountain communities bridges are tremendously important.
So this little town meeting, this very gem of democracy, was faced with this problem. But they were also faced with the problem of educating their local youth.
In a mountain town with flash floods roaring over the banks of its watercourses after hard rains, bridges have an imperious priority. Our bridges needed reinforcement, not only from recurring high water, but against the great tonnage of modern traffic. It would be dangerous not to rebuild them. It would take all the resources of a
Loans to Students
poor mountain town to keep our bridges in repair. To add to that expense the enormous cost of a new school-insane.
The tangible needs of the body and the impalpable needs of the mind and spirit stood up to see which was the stronger. The material needs outshouted the ideal. They sounded real and actual. The little flickering flame of responsibility for the future of the town's children died down to a faint glimmer in the hearts of the men and women whose votes would in a few moments make the decision.
Then up sprang Patrick Thompson, the son of an immigrant, and he said:
"We are being told that our town cannot afford to keep its bridges safe and also to provide for its children a preparation for life that will give them a fair chance alongside other American children.
That's what we are being told. Not one of us here really believes it. We just can't think what to say back. But suppose it were true-Then I say, if we have to choose, 'Let the bridges fall down.' What kind of a town would we rather have, 50 years from now-a place where nitwit folks go back and forth over good bridges? Or a town with brainy, well-educated people capable of holding their own in the modem way of life? You know which of those two is really wanted by every one of us here. I say, 'Let the bridges fall down.' "
That is also my scales of priorities. I support the government in this step and I hope it will be one of many which will follow, longer, more venturesome and more helpful in this important field of education.

speechtext:
It seems to me that it is only in times of emergency that we do things really well. In 1939 we took a sluggish, feeble economy and built it into an efficient economic machine. In the years immediately after the war we introduced a plan for the education of veterans of which thousands of Canadians, some young and some not so young, were able to take advantage. I wonder where we would be today in the staffing of our professions if that plan had not been undertaken. There must be thousands of teachers, doctors, scientists, lawyers and accountants who, but for this scheme, would have been unable to receive an education qualifying them for those positions. Now, only a relatively few years later, the plan has virtually come to an end and we are back to the old way of doing things.
This situation means that students of high ability do not as a rule encounter much difficulty. They are equipped intellectually to benefit from all the best scholarships. Again, students who come from high income homes do not have very much trouble. But the vast majority of Canadian students are in neither of these categories; they are the ordinary people who staff our offices and classrooms, go into general medical practices and fill our professions, and for many of them getting through university represents a difficult struggle.
There are certain things which I think we should do on a national basis. Certain things are already done on a national basis, and they are done quite well. Unemployment insurance is handled on a national basis and I do not think anyone now would want it to be otherwise. Hospital planning is a subject of fairly successful joint federal-provincial arrangements. Family allowances are handled on a national basis and the proposed pension plan will be handled in this way except for some compromise about the allocation of funds which, I think, is unfortunate. We should consider doing other things on a national basis. We always run into a constitutional problem whenever education is discussed in this parliament. I do not know of any country which is so cursed with constitutional problems and arguments as is Canada. I know as well as anyone else that section 93 does give jurisdiction in this field to the provinces and I will express my own personal views at this point because I think

my party, along with others, still believes in the principle of section 93. I am not advocating that all levels of education should be under the jurisdiction of the federal government. But I do think the level of higher or post-secondary education as mentioned in the bill could well be a federal responsibility. I say this because in the first place I believe most Canadians will accept it. Many spokesmen, particularly from Quebec, might tell me differently. They may be right; I am not sure. But I am quite sure of my opinion that in the English speaking provinces the majority would not object and might even favour federal jurisdiction over higher or university education, and perhaps over technical and vocational education as well. In the second place, the provinces do not do a particularly good job in this field. The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman) put it bluntly yesterday. He said it was a big flop as far as the provinces are concerned and he quoted figures to show how poorly they supported university financing. I think the federal authority could do a better job.
Again, students travel widely among the provinces in the course of getting their education. Certain universities specialize in particular fields and I see nothing wrong about the movement which takes place both at graduate and undergraduate level. In addition, the federal government is already involved in the field of education at the present time. In the public accounts committee the other day the staff of treasury board presented us with a list of federal subsidies. It is entitled "Provision in estimates for grants, subsidies and special payments" and I shall refer only to those which deal with education. Under the heading of education and research, for the fiscal year 1964-65 the total amount of money to be expended by the federal government is $156,288,800. This is down, unfortunately, from 1963-64, when the figure was $204,948,290. The federal government now makes available, in direct grants to universities, $27,226,000; and grants to universities for research amount to $25,195,000. For other types of research the amount is $3,038,500; for scholarships, fellowships, etc., the amount is $74,700; and for vocational training and other types of training in that field the figure is $100,754,600. So the government is well into this field.
I realize that this question of federal participation in education is a touchy one and we hear many speeches against it; but I think that during this debate is the time for this view to be expressed, because many Cana-
Loans to Students
dians hold this view. Quite frankly, for the benefit of the hon. member for Joliette-L'As-somption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) and some others, in this field I am a centralizer and I would like to see established a federal office of education.
A number of people have said recently that we should examine the priorities of this country. I believe the suggestion came from the premier of Manitoba-the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) mentioned it the other day, and the Toronto Globe and Mail mentioned it this morning in their editorial-that there are many demands at the present time for higher education, pensions, medical care programs resulting from the recent report of the Hall commission, and that we should have a conference to examine which of these subjects should have priority. The suggestion implied there is that we cannot afford all these things. I should like to dispute that particular implication. Canada certainly can afford these things. I was recently checking over the budgets of the past ten years-that is for the years between 1954 and 1963-and I noted that, in round figures, during that period this country spent approximately $15 billion on the Department of National Defence budget. That is $15 billion in a ten year period-and that is a conservative estimate; the actual figures are higher. Of that $15 billion, $470 million were spent for the development of the CF-104 aircraft, and it was scrapped. There was some value out of that program because some people received wages and salaries cheques out of it, but it did not have very much more value. Approximately $40 million was spent on the development of the army vehicle called the Bobcat, and that was scrapped. Again, the only benefit to the country was derived from the wages certain people received. There was no lasting benefit.
I suggest that this country, which can spend $15 billion in a ten year period on defence of very doubtful value, can afford a program of higher education and provide assistance to students in regard to the tuition fees they are paying; we can afford to provide a living allowance; we can afford a medical care program. We in Canada can afford these things if we want to; and if we continue not doing these things, it must be an indication that we do not want to do them.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in considering this bill respecting loans to students, and in listening to some speeches from other Quebec members in the

Loans to Students
house, I can only stop and think that the part played here by a member from the province of Quebec is far from being a sinecure, and that it becomes more and more difficult to take a decision in the present context. This is due, partly to the fact-and other members will agree with me-that the text of the constitution has been appreciably influenced by the presence of a concentration of French Canadians in Quebec. As a matter of fact, I doubt very much if the British North America Act would have been written in the same way, had it not been for the existence of the French fact in Quebec.
In the beginning of confederation it did not appear that there was overlapping in jurisdiction, but as Canada's progress developed and as a result of the two world wars, the British North America Act has become for some people a kind of barrier that hindered Canada's progress. That is when we saw, in almost every field, the central government skirt around this barrier in order to solve some problems. However, the provinces did just as much in the field of indirect taxation rights.
It was normal that following this change of attitude, the Quebec members became not only the law makers, but also the watchdogs of the constitution in the house, in the same way that it is normal for the members for Yukon and the Northwest Territories to champion the interests of the population of those areas.
Decentralization is more and more to the fore, and whenever the word "decentralization" is mentioned we obviously come up against certain political and economic theories. But I am sure that if we wish Canada to remain a federation, and if we want all the provinces to remain within such a federation, this is the course we must take. Besides, it has been proven that excessive centralization becomes ineffective.
Does this mean that in order to govern, the provinces must adhere to such a principle of decentralization in their education system? Not at all, Mr. Speaker; on the contrary, in the province of Quebec, for instance, the whole of the educational system is being more and more centralized. Results have shown that centralization to a certain extent may be good, but how hard it can be sometimes to reach a happy medium.
I remember an editorial by Andre Lauren-deau, in Le Devoir, which gives us a good idea of the changes going on in the province of Quebec. I quote:

Toward the end of the nineteenth century, when the authorities of the province of Quebec decided to vote $100,000 for the teaching of sciences in our universities, McGill took its share and took to sciences; Laval University saw fit to draw up a brief showing the dangers resulting from the intrusion of the state into the educational field and did not take up the teaching of sciences.
Today, in 1964, education in the province of Quebec is controlled by a minister of education. There is no more talk of the danger resulting from the intrusion of the state into the educational field. The importance of the school boards is gradually decreasing. Many of them were merged and must be grouped in regional schools to provide high school teaching. Why should we have this centralization of powers? Because only the government could finance an educational system that would be open to all Quebeckers.
Since the provinces really look after education, there is no doubt that the federal government will be less and less justified in interfering and, as a matter of fact, it will intervene less and less. Some provinces had no student loans plans, others already had such a plan, but there is no doubt that those loans were insufficient, judging from the enthusiasm which this legislation stirred up among the people.
Mr. Speaker, if today the government controls education in Quebec, it is because the government finances it.
If today Quebec fears the presence of the federal government in the field of education, it is for the same reasons. It is because it fears the federal government will succeed in controlling education in the Quebec territory.
Let us be quite frank about it, when you pay for something, you hope in return to control what you pay for.
On the other hand, if this causes no constitutional problems outside Quebec, has the province of Quebec the right to deprive the rest of Canada by sabotaging legislation which could be profitable? I think this would be ridiculous. The provinces which do not want the plan proposed by the central government should not be penalized because they refuse to adhere to it. On the contrary, after the usual consultations, a formula should be devised which would allow a province wishing to look after this herself to receive its share of the fund which the central government puts at the disposal of the country. That is what the present government did as regards municipal loans and that is what we are doing with student loans.

I do not think, constitutionally, Ottawa could be accused of using its credit power to put at the disposal of the provinces the funds they need to fulfil their constitutional obligations.
We have done so in the case of youth allowances by allowing the province of Quebec a further abatement of 3 per cent personal income tax.
In the present case, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), on behalf of the federal government, agrees to make available to the provinces which will not adhere to the plan, the equivalent of the expenditures involved for the administration of the present act by the provinces.
In other words, the guarantee of the loans and the repayment of interests will be assumed by the federal government, but all decisions as well as control and administration will be left to the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, some members, including myself, would have preferred this legislation to be introduced in the framework of a redistribution of income between the central government and the provinces.
Today some hon. members would prefer that the central government should not interfere in this field already occupied by the provinces or the majority of them; nevertheless, nobody can say that the central government has not given the provinces complete freedom to adhere or not to this system, without, for that matter, being penalized.
By choosing this solution the province of Quebec, far from quitting confederation, as some have alleged, on the contrary, is enabled to remain within confederation and to benefit therefrom, while keeping the special status conferred upon her by the constitution.
This new formula, apparently acceptable to the majority, needs no doubt to be improved to allow the initiative for some future projects to be taken here by the provinces as much as by the federal government; otherwise, this formula will before long become another cause for dissatisfaction.
Mr. Speaker, yesterday when the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanau-diere (Mr. Paul) shouted the word "scandal" and I only said "Oh, oh", he remarked before the house that the member for Longueuil should have spent some months at a university. I may reply to the hon. member that being one of ten children, I might perhaps have had an opportunity to attend university if the present legislation concerning students' loans had been in effect when I was of school age. But no, I had to go to
Loans to Students
work when I was 15 and take evening classes in order to complete my education and so that my brothers could attend university.
Such cases are found every day in our country and that is why I tell those who are against the bill for certain principles, that the human factor must also be kept in mind when we are legislating.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I say that no one will deny that the people concerned, that is the young ones, who are trying in every possible way and who sometimes have to overcome great difficulties in order to get an education, are grateful for this initiative and I do not think we can oppose it. So long as there is one Canadian who does not have the financial means to complete his education, the governments will fall short of their responsibility.

Mr. Speaker, in his epilogue to a recent book called "Paths of American Thought", Arthur N. Schlesinger, Jr. quotes Professor J. K. Galbraith as having readily observed that a dollar or a rupee invested in the intellectual improvement of human beings will likely bring a greater increase in national income than a dollar or a rupee devoted to railways, dams, machine tools or other tangible capital goods. It seems to me that this statement is a reasonable context in which to discuss this bill for a minute or two. As I have observed from listening to the speeches of other hon. members in the house, it is a bill which will induce support from most. But I want to suggest-and I am sure the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) recognizes this fact -that this bill by no means solves the problems of higher education in Canada, and I am sure the minister or the government do not expect this to be the case.
I agree with the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) that I do not think we have any apology to make for the time we take over the bill. It has certainly been refreshing to me to hear that occasionally this house can discuss an issue in which in some cases fairly strong different points of view are expressed, and yet we can keep pretty close to the main philosophy behind the proposed measure. As some of us are interested in the image of parliament, I should like to say I think this improves our image and I should like to congratulate at least those who have participated in the debate up to now.

Loans to Students
By coincidence, while we have been here in Ottawa discussing the student loan legislation the Canadian college of teachers has been meeting at Lac Beauport, Quebec-and they have been luckier there than we have been here, perhaps. I think one of the speeches reported in the Montreal Star of July 14 is pertinent. The speech was made by Dr. Floyd G. Robinson, director of the Canadian council for research in education. On the 13th of July he called Canada "the intellectual beggar among the educationally advanced countries of the world". In his speech he went on to say:
-part of the solution to the void in research must come from increased centralization of educational matters. "Educational leadership in Canada will require that we cure our schizophrenic ambivalence on the matter of federal and provincial responsibilities in education.. .When functions which are properly central are decentralized, the result can only be confusion, inefficiency and a pretence of independence based upon a peculiar assumption that a decision made in ignorance is an independent decision."
But Dr. Robinson hastened to add that he was "not advocating a federal system of education, but only that we do not sacrifice the possibilities of genuine Canadian leadership in education to an outdated theory of educational organization."
He decried the fact that Canada spent less than one tenth of 1 per cent of its total educational budget for research.
I think that is an apt statement and it is interesting to me that it comes during the time we are discussing this bill.
One or two points have been made about the bill itself that I should like to emphasize. I think it was the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner) who hoped that the minister through the regulations would ensure that the policy of mobility of students is kept intact. "Intact" is a bad word to use when I have just referred to mobility, but in any event the principle of mobility of students should be remembered and encouraged. I underline this point as a member of parliament from the maritime provinces. If we can claim nothing else for the maritimes, I think we can claim to have contributed over the years to the higher education of a good many people in this country holding positions of leadership in many fields.
Most of the judges of British Columbia.

Somebody says "most of the judges of British Columbia", and there are many other people, including the recently appointed deputy to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I do not want to catalogue these achievements. My modesty would

prevent that. But we in the maritimes have always felt that our educational institutions have been very much enriched because of the number of students from other parts of Canada who have been able to come to the maritimes to get their higher education, and we hope that policy will be continued under this legislation.
The other point made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George that I thought worthy of note was that some formula must be worked out to take care of part time students, and that on the basis of the experience that will evolve from this legislation we must make provision eventually for night students and so on. Perhaps the minister has that in mind now. I should like to emphasize that point. There are a great many people who are getting their education at night in many of our institutions of higher learning.
Would the hon. member permit a question on this very point? Would he not agree that the object of this legislation would be to get part time students to return to a full time students role?

I think that is a reasonable suggestion, but there are some who cannot do so because of their family or personal situations. I do not think $1,000 will permit a man with a family to leave his daily vocation and go to university, but I think the point is well worth considering.
I want to emphasize one other point that was made very forcibly by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin). I suspect that by now the justice department or the advisers to the minister have reached some solution, or I assume they have, because in my modest opinion clauses 2 (b) and 2 (k) of the bill are completely ultra vires and their passage would seriously affect the usefulness of the legislation. I know I cannot ask the minister questions at this stage but I hope we will hear soon from the treasury benches of a satisfactory amendment to these now quite inoperative provisions.
As the hon. member for Greenwood has pointed out, section 65 of the British North America Act sets out the responsibilities of the lieutenant governor in council quite clearly and, if I may put it this way, to my knowledge there is really only one person, using the word "person" in a general sense, concerning whom this parliament cannot legislate or delegate legislation to, and that is the lieutenant governor in council. I must say I am surprised that the bill has reached this stage in this form. I hope we can be reassured

on this matter soon. I would hope that nobody would challenge the constitutionality of the legislation because all that would do would be to delay the attainment of a desirable objective; but I cannot understand how the bill reached this stage in the unconstitutional form in which it now appears before us.
Because this is a debating forum and we are expected to learn from those who have intimate knowledge on various matters, I should like some guidance on clause 15 of the bill and why the government feels that clause 15 is constitutional. I presume they are going to rely on the banking provisions in section 91 of the B.N.A. Act, but I should like to be instructed how this jibes with the property and civil rights aspect, which is a provincial responsibility under the act. In any event, I will be glad to hear their views. If clause 15 raises a debatable point, and I concede it is debatable, I do not think for one minute that clauses 2 (b) and 2 (k) are debatable at all. Some work has to be done on them and an amendment proposed, or else the act will be in serious constitutional trouble.
There have been a few radical suggestions made and I suppose a backbench Tory can make a radical suggestion. I think it should be mandatory for the bank to make the loan, once a certificate of eligibility has been granted. I do not think the giving or denying of a loan can be properly left to bank managers, particularly in view of the fact that this statute will apply to people who have been in Canada only a short time as well as people who are citizens. I would hate to think that the fate of the borrower would always be in the hands of the bank manager. As somebody has said, there is no safer or better investment for a bank than a loan guaranteed as to principal and interest by the government of Canada, and which also is insured. Once a certificate of eligibility has been granted the choice of a bank should be left to the student, but after that point the bank should make the loan.
Otherwise there are going to be different classes of students, and the student who comes to this country from another country and stays here for a year, who has not in any way really established his credit under the magic formula that banks use for granting credit, is going to be in a less favourable position than one who has been in the community for generations or whose family has.
I, too, have been intrigued with the arguments concerning the constitutional position vis-a-vis the whole philosophy behind the bill. I am intrigued by this business of hav-
Loans to Students
ing one minute a bogeyman brought out about the constitution and the next minute having, with all respect to the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie), this false altar of centralization brought out. I like to go between these two, being a reasonably minded Conservative. I cannot understand for one minute how a loan granted by a bank which allows a student to pursue higher education in the university of his choice, in the language of his choice, if you like in the culture of his choice, and the discipline of his choice, can be considered to be an infringement of section 93 of the British North America Act. In my opinion, this bill reinforces the very independence that those who espouse another culture in this country are quite rightly trying to keep inviolate. The government is not telling them what they are going to study, how they are going to study or where they are going to study. All the government is doing is providing the money, by way of these loans, so that this can be done. With the greatest of respect to some of my own colleagues and to others who have pulled out the drums on this issue, I cannot see how it applies.
I believe some day we will have to-
A special province.

I recognize that-well, I am not going to start a debate here with my friend. I should like to remind the minister, if he needs reminding, of the submission made to him by the Canadian universities foundation in December, 1963, which was partly a resubmission of a brief this foundation submitted to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in May, 1963. I know this point has been made by others, but I think it is worth emphasizing. In the brief to the Prime Minister of Canada in May, 1963, the foundation says:
-we pointed out that the total requirement of capital for universities and colleges, and for the creation of research facilities in university-affiliated teaching hospitals, for the three years 196364 to 1965-66, would be approximately $800 million. Estimates indicate that at the present rate of spending for these purposes, the governments of the provinces might be expected to contribute something less than $300 million towards this total and that $100 million might be expected as gifts and donations from corporations and individuals. If it may be assumed that the additional loan funds needed for university residential accommodation (about $100 million during that period) will be available from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the remaining need still totals more than $300 million for the three year period.

Loans to Students
The final paragraph of the part I propose quoting that has application to this part of my remarks is as follows:
In that brief we suggested that the government of Canada establish a fund of $300 million for matching capital grants to universities and colleges. We wish to confirm the need and state that the urgency has now been compounded.
Well, if the need was compounded in December, 1963, by the inexorable laws of compounding it must be even worse today. This was emphasized again in the 1963-64 report of the Canada Council. In their introductory remarks the Canada Council gives a very useful recent history of the crisis conditions through which universities have been passing in the last few years. I quote from page 36:
Most of the older faculties have expanded at a remarkable rate and new colleges and faculties have sprung up everywhere, filling old gaps in our educational establishment and meeting the demands of the newer disciplines. The rapid growth of our institutions, however, has brought many problems in its train. First, there is the difficulty of recruiting the many teachers so urgently required to meet the increasing demand. And there is, of course, the special problem of finding experts in some of the newer disciplines, who will be able to give form and leadership to departments and institutes that the country has begun to need.
We have the Canadian universities foundation, we have the Canada Council, and if we need any more witnesses we have the Canadian school trustees association. In their brief presented to the royal commission on taxation they have a proposal. I am not going to go through the figures because we have had them, but I think one of the proposals is of interest. They recommended that there be a division of responsibility for financing-I think the word "financing" should be underlined before we run into the constitutional wall-education among the three levels of government. Local governments would be responsible for elementary education; provincial governments for secondary education and the federal government for higher education and vocational education. I believe this suggestion is at least worthy of thought. I think probably in the final analysis it is a little too neat.
However I believe the proposal to have higher education a federal responsibility is one that is compelling to me. This is the last thing I want to say, that in a very interesting speech given on November 28, 1963, Dean J. F. McCreary, dean of the faculty of medicine of the University of British Columbia, spoke of the urgent need from the point of view of graduate schools for capital, particularly in view of the fact this problem is going

to be accentuated if the recommendations of the royal commission on health services is implemented.
If I may sum up, I should like to say I will vote for this bill. I will vote for it in the knowledge it really does not meet the Liberal party platform, but that does not disturb me because very little legislation we have had so far does meet it. Second, we must remind ourselves when we boastfully congratulate ourselves about this wonderful legislation that it really does not meet the needs of higher education one bit. I hope that clause 2(b) and (k), which in my opinion are now quite badly drafted and in fact are unconstitutional, will be subject to the proper amendment.
