speechtext: Order. It being five o'clock the house will now proceed to the consideration of private members' business as listed on today's order paper, namely private bills, notices of motions (papers), and public bills.

subtopic: CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE

speechtext: Bill No. S-34, to incorporate Nova Scotia Savings and Loan Company.-Mr. Regan.

The house in committee on Bill No. S-28, respecting The Quebec Board of Trade-Mr. Cantin-Mr. Batten in the chair.
On clause 1-Preamble.

Mr. Chairman, as I had to
leave the sitting when this bill was submitted to the committee on banking and commerce, I had delegated the representation I might make to the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Frenette).
Later on I was told that it was believed in certain quarters that the members of the Quebec board of trade had succeeded in suppressing my arguments against this organization calling itself the board of trade of metropolitan Quebec.
That is why I feel, more particularly because various chambers of commerce gave me very definite instructions that I should give some explanations and justify my intended opposition to the bill.
We have now before us a bill which was amended by the committee on banking and commerce, so that the arguments which might be made for the term "metropolitan" are perhaps not exactly the same as those

which might be advanced against the Quebec and district o f Quebec board of trade using the new term of "district of Quebec".
Though I do not want to read them out, Mr. Chairman, I wish to say that I received letters and telegrams from the chambers of commerce of the Quebec-Montmorency and Quebec-Charlevoix areas, from Antoine Hamel, director of the Charlesbourg chamber of commerce, from Louis Warren, secretary, from Marcel Pageau, president of the chamber of commerce of Loretteville, from Camille Theberge, president of the chamber of commerce of Courville, from the chamber of commerce of Beauport, and from Robert Legare, president of the chamber of commerce of the county of Portneuf.
Mr. Chairman, before this bill was referred to the committee on banking and commerce, all those chambers of commerce were against the board of trade of the city of Quebec, whose territory, field of activity and headquarters have always been limited to the city of Quebec, using the expression "metropolitan Quebec", which, according to the dictionary, could apply to an extension of jurisdiction on the part of the board of trade of Quebec.
When you consider that metropolitan Quebec extends on the south shore to Levis, Lauzon, St. Romuald, etc., as well as, on the north shore, to various parishes or to the municipalities of Charlevoix, Quebec, Montmorency and the county of Portneuf, you realize that it amounts to quite a large extension of jurisdiction.
Despite this change in name, the board of trade says it has no intention of extending its jurisdiction over those various localities. It simply wants to enjoy the prestige of an enlarged board, covering a whole metropolitan area.
I feel that the arguments in favour of that change, if they do not hide anything special, are not worth much, because Quebec can be considered as the name of the province of Quebec, of the city of Quebec and also of the Quebec area.
I would like to point out something else, Mr. Chairman, while I think about it. The report and the minutes of proceedings of the committee on banking and commerce, which should contain the evidence given before that committee, have not yet been published. Usually, the English version is distributed immediately and the French version is available six or ten days later, and sometimes still later.
We do not even have the report of this committee available at present, so that it is
Private Bills
difficult to refer to it, especially when I did not attend the sittings, so as to know what arguments were put forward in favour of this bill.
On the other hand, I obtained the minutes of the Senate committee on banking and commerce where Mr. Renault St-Laurent, barrister, appearing on behalf of the Quebec board of trade, had put forward several arguments in favour of the change in name. He pointed out, among other things that at least 5,000 persons write every year to the Quebec board of trade, which shows that this organization covers a much greater territory than that of Quebec city.
If the Quebec board of trade is so important and has so much influence, I fail to see why it seeks to have its name changed even if the latter makes no mention of metropolitan Quebec. According to Mr. Renault St-Laurent, barrister, it is merely to give legal recognition to a long standing situation and he gave several examples. He said that it was the Quebec board of trade which brought about the establishment of several companies, not only in the city of Quebec itself, but in the area also. I agree with him on that. He further stated that many of the board's members-in fact, a large number of them-come from outside Quebec city. I have no quarrel with that either, but it proves nothing.
I belong to the Montreal medical association and I am quite willing to pay my membership fee, because I feel it is advantageous for me to belong to that association. However, that does not mean I would be ready to give the Montreal medical association the right to represent the interests of Quebec doctors.
That is why the arguments invoked are very weak in my opinion, the more so since it is claimed:

They have made several studies of reports on the port of Quebec. They have a jurisdiction over the office of the port warden which they have exercised practically since the port warden was appointed by Ottawa and they are responsible for recommending the person who is to be appointed port warden and any assistants.

Then, it seems that the board of trade has great influence in the Quebec harbour.
I should like to take this opportunity to say that the Quebec harbour, which should be a metropolitan harbour including much more than the city of Quebec, denies to every individual who does not live in the city

Private Bills
oi Quebec the right to be employed as longshoreman, because of the international longshoremen's association, local 1739. This is a very serious situation. I have pointed out that fact on a few occasions to the Minister of Labour, but he told me that he had no authority over a local union.
As I was saying, Quebec harbour should be considered as part of an area much larger than Quebec city. The minister added that the union was not allowed to accept members not residing in Quebec city. It is a fact that in an answer given by a union official mentioned the "city card". He said that an individual must have his "city card", in other words, be a resident of Quebec city. He also said that, if Montreal did not find it advisable to eliminate this requirement, he did not see why Quebec should.
Therefore, I believe this is a discriminatory requirement which the board of trade should have considered long ago, but which it apparently forgot.
It seems that this board of trade, like most of the others, is more interested in the large companies who are members paying membership fees and that the interests of those companies strangely converge towards the interests of the board of trade.
I heard that, following a meeting which took place when the committee on banking and commerce was sitting, every party was apparently satisfied with the amendment made. Therefore, I shall not be more demanding than the companies themselves. I will not go farther than those company officials agreed to go.
I simply want to protest, and I have supporting evidence, against the fact that the Quebec board of trade is enlarging upon its jurisdiction. Besides, I wonder why they want to have an enlarged jurisdiction, when it is only a question of promoting the interests of the city and district.
They go even further. In clause 3 of the bill, it is said:
-and of the province of Quebec and Canada in general-
Then, obviously, one cannot object to that. If that is the kind of jurisdiction they want, there is no objection. However, they go a little further. In clause 3 (c), the corporation wishes and shall be empowered to:
-to organize, if necessary, a stock exchange and to promote the centralization of the grain, produce, provision and other trades in the city and metropolitan area of Quebec.
[Mr. Marcoux.j
Paragraph (e) also states:
-to adjust, settle and determine disputes, controversies and misunderstandings arising between persons engaged in the same trade or business, or which may be submitted to arbitration as hereinafter provided:
This has already started. The board of trade, at the request or probably with the co-operation of the city of Quebec, decided to study the problem of closing hours for businesses in the Quebec area. One knows that the city of Quebec has very strict and very rigid regulations about closing hours. Many industries which come to the Quebec area or district, or to metropolitan Quebec, decide to open stores in areas where they do not have to abide by closing hours imposed by the city of Quebec.
Under the pretext that these stores are prejudicial to the city of Quebec, the new stores are to be prevented from opening at hours allowed in various municipalities. Of course, it is impossible to obtain unanimous consent.
I know that in my own city, like in many others, the boards of trade as well as the municipalities themselves are against such a move. The board of trade of Quebec district, which was previously the board of trade of metropolitan Quebec, wants to submit a study showing that all municipalities around Quebec including Levis, Lauzon and St. Romuald should be subject to identical closing hours.
You can see, Mr. Chairman, that this could be detrimental to the municipalities adjoining Quebec city. It may be that the city of Quebec was ill-administered for a number of years, but it is not up to the adjoining municipalities to replenish the municipality of Quebec if the latter was unable to attract industries in its area, within its own territory.
If the other municipalities have succeeded in attracting industries in their area-even though it would be on account of the Quebec board of trade-I fail to see why the local boards of trade would be prevented from expressing their opinion, for instance about closing time or about something else.
In my own constituency, there is, for instance, the problem related to sand bars on the Beaupre shore. Many municipalities all along this shore, and their boards of trade, are very much interested in that problem. I feel that the wish expressed by these boards of trade may not be the same as that expressed by the Quebec board of trade.
If these boards of trade ever make any representations to the government for the settlement of this question and in favour of

the municipalities ol the Beaupre coast, the city of Quebec, through the Quebec district board of trade, may make representations to the contrary, not only to the government but also to the various local boards of trade to determine the limits of the area.
Moreover, Mr. Chairman, as I was saying a while ago, the boards of trade federation of the counties of Charlevoix, Quebec, Montmorency and Portneuf represent a greater number of people than those served by the Quebec board of trade.
It is said that the Quebec board of trade does not want to encroach upon the powers of the local chambers of commerce and that it will let the latter look after the local problems. This is precisely another point which will make this difficult, for who will decide whether a problem is local, metropolitan, regional or a district problem. That question is hard to settle. It could be settled under the Quebec and Quebec district board of trade charter which perhaps will create some difficulties to local chambers of commerce. I wish to put on record that the president of the Quebec board of trade, Mr. Louis Dus-seault, and also, Mr. Talbot, of the same body, assured me that the Quebec board of trade will in no way deal with problems pertaining to local boards and to the district board, such as the board of trades federation of the Quebec area.
In that case, Mr. Chairman, as I said earlier, the suggestions made by the various representatives who appeared before the committee on banking and commerce must be accepted. I should like to put on record, however, that if at any time the Quebec board of trade and the Quebec district board of trade attempt to infringe upon rights not belonging to them, when it is understood, of course, that it is not a matter of jurisdiction, but only a matter of trade and industrial promotion, so that local boards can say: Here, we see in Hansard of the House of Commons a promise made by Mr. Louis Dusseault, Mr. Talbot and others that this board of trade will not encroach on the rights of local boards. Then, it may give them a place to meet where they can really prepare an opposition to some possible intrusion by the Quebec board of trade.
Once again, Mr. Chairman, I am going to support the bill any way, on division, but I want to say that personally, I object, and for various reasons, and I could go into every detail of the many reasons which militate against the fact that the house accepted

the name "Quebec district board of trade", while it is the Quebec city board of trade. And we specially protest against their method of going ahead which mostly looked like a hiding game when they said they wanted benefits they already had. I always wondered why they wanted benefits they already had, while things could be left as they were.
That explains my stand, but I do not want to delay the business of the house any longer.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?

Mr. Chairman, this bill gives authority to the Bell Telephone Company to augment its board of directors. Before the bill passes I have a few remarks I should like to make.
A telephone company of necessity operates in certain areas of the country a monopolistic business. This is a necessity with which I think no one would quarrel. It would obviously be completely impracticable to try and run competitive telephone companies over the same area. On the other hand monopolies are not looked on with favour in our form of competitive society.
Under these circumstances, where a company is operating a business which must be run in a monopolistic fashion there are generally three options which are open to deal with such a problem. In the first instance, the service could be provided by a government department. As an example, we have our postal service supplied by a department of the federal government. It could be operated as a crown corporation. Or it can be operated as a closely regulated private company. Personally, in this instance I favour a crown corporation, but I do not intend to argue the merits or demerits of this particular point.
It seems to me that if we are going to have a private company operating in a monopolistic fashion, it must be regulated, and it must

be properly regulated. It must be regulated so that the shareholders, who in this instance are widely scattered and come from all walks of life in the country, have their interests protected. But in addition to the shareholders, the users of the service, the subscribers, the people who pay the telephone bills, must have their interests protected too. To me this is the paramount consideration. There was a statement made in the house when dealing with the administration of justice to the effect that not only must justice be done but it must appear to be done. I think the same principle is applicable in dealing with the problem of a company such as the Bell Telephone Company. When we think of the rates which you, Mr. Chairman, myself and others across the country pay for our telephone service, not only must the rates be fair but they must also appear to be fair.
Evidence was taken in regard to this bill before the standing committe on railways, canals and telegraph lines, and I have before me the minutes of proceedings and evidence, volume 4, of the sitting which was held on July 7, 1964. During the course of those hearings a number of questions and problems were raised which in turn raised doubts in my mind about the fairness of the rate structure and the operations of the company. I am not going to go into all of them, and I should like to make it completely clear that I am not saying or suggesting that there are inequities in the way in which the company is operating. What I am saying however is that doubts are raised in my mind in connection with some aspects of the operation of the company, and I think in view of the nature of their business these doubts should be cleared up.
As we do not have too much time, the doubts I want to deal with fall into only two areas. The first area relates to the question of rates charged by the telephone company. There were several facts brought out in the evidence. At page 427 of the proceedings the hon. member for Three Rivers, the former minister of transport, brought out the fact that those who are serviced by the Bell Telephone Company in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario pay more than those serviced by nationalized companies in western provinces such as Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta.
It was stated by the president of the company that the cost to subscribers in large metropolitan areas was of necessity higher than the cost to those in smaller communities.

The reason was said to be that an individual subscriber in a community where there were more connections, could make more calls on a local basis, and would thus pay more for his calls as costs were higher. This may well be the fact, but as an engineer with a little background in manufacturing it has always been to me a principle that as volume increases cost reduces, and there are some economies of scale. Now, it may be that the argument presented by the president of the company is perfectly valid, I do not know, but it has raised a doubt in my mind.
At page 430 of the evidence, when reference was made to long distance rates, the president of the company stated that long distance charges in Canada were higher than those in the United States. The reason given was that the lines are strung over great areas of less densely populated country, and therefore the cost per subscriber for long distance calls was higher. A little further on, at page 433, the hon. member for Three Rivers, who as former minister of transport I think should be aware of these circumstances, said that long distance charges in the prairie provinces by those companies operated by the provinces are lower than charges in Ontario and Quebec. Now, surely we have fewer people in the prairies than we have in Ontario and Quebec, so this appears to be the exact opposite of the argument advanced by the president of the company in stating the reason for the charges being higher in Canada than in the United States. Again, there may be adequate explanation for this problem, I do not know; but it raises doubts in my mind.
The second area I should like to deal with which also causes doubts in my mind is the situation with respect to Northern Electric, which is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Bell Telephone Company. Northern Electric gained a charter under a section of their act of incorporation which, as reported at page 417 of the committee report, reads as follows:
The company shall also have power to enter into any arrangement with any person or company possessing, as proprietor, any line of telegraphic or telephonic communication, or any power or right to use communication by means of the telephone upon such terms-
And so on and so forth. In effect then, Bell have been able to acquire Northern Electric under its charter because Northern operated,
I gather, approximately four miles of telephone line.
Northern Electric has since that date been expanded to a manufacturing giant, a company which is doing some $300 million worth
Private Bills
of business a year. Half of this business is sales of manufactured products to the Bell Telephone Company itself. The other half is outside, what I call commercial sales to the trade generally. I have absolutely no argument against Bell doing as much manufacturing as it wants to. It has its own "make or buy" decisions to reach based on economic considerations, which should properly be the responsibility of the management of that company. It is their job to ensure the lowest cost possible, and this sort of "make or buy" consideration is entirely a managerial responsibility. But it seems to me to be a perversion of the original intention of the legislation for Bell to take a company with four miles of telephone line and use that as the basis for acquiring it, and then to swing that company into a manufacturing enterprise doing $150 million worth of business each year on an open and competitive basis outside the field of telephone communication in this country. I am not questioning the legality of this operation; it is probably perfectly legal, but it does appear to me to be a perversion of the original intent of the legislation.
Apparently in investigating the rate structure of the Bell Telephone Company the board of transport commissioners investigated to some degree the relationship between Bell and Northern. Again, if I may refer to the evidence in the committee, page 426, it is stated by Mr. Scrivener of the company that the Northern Electric Company reports to the board of transport commissioners and he then outlines the basis on which they provide information, in these words:
It has been based on financial considerations such as an examination of the records, the profits and the non-profits, during these applications. You will see it in the report of the Bell. Bell reports continuously to the board of transport commissioners, but Northern does not.
The question that is raised in my mind is. in what detail does Northern report to the board of transport commissioners? Northern has an annual report and I have a copy of that annual report here. The annual report indicates the profitability of Northern but it does not in any way indicate a breakdown between the business Northern does with Bell Telephone and the business Northern does in the open, competitive, commercial market. Does the board of transport commissioners, when it is examining rate applications by Bell Telephone, examine the relationship of these two parts of the business that Northern is doing? I do not know whether it does, but

Private Bills
I think we should have some satisfaction on this point because to me the danger exists that an unfair situation could be created.
Again I want to emphasize the fact that I am not saying this situation does exist. I think we should be sure it does not, but I have had nothing to indicate that we are sure on that point. The danger lies in the fact that $150 million of the Bell Telephone Company's material supply comes form Northern. On the basis of the cost of this material Bell makes application for the telephone rates that you and I and every telephone subscriber have to pay. I do not say this happens but it is possible that Northern could sell its commercial products on the outside market at low prices to drive out competition, penetrate the market totally and possibly eliminate competition ultimately and could subsidize that operation by charging higher prices to the Bell Telephone Company. These prices would then be paid in effect through the telephone rates set by the board of transport commissioners as the result of Bell's rate applications and would be paid by you and I and every other telephone subscriber. In effect we would then be subsidizing Northern in their attempt to drive out competition in a certain segment of the market.
I do not say this is happening but if it did happen it is something that would be seriously wrong, and I think it is important enough that we should be absolutely sure that this does not and cannot occur. There is no guarantee that it does but again there is no guarantee that it does not.
In the evidence there were indications that there were cross-checks with the prices to outside purchasers on the basis of which Northern sold to Bell. Knowing the nature of the business I would doubt that purchasers other than Bell who buy telephone equipment from Northern would have any other sources to which they could go for their equipment. Therefore I wonder whether this is really an effective cross-check against the prices at which Bell buys its equipment from Northern. Again I do not know.
I know. I will prove it.

We as members of parliament have allowed a monopoly to exist in this country and it may be that this monopoly in this situation is to the advantage of all concerned. But it is important to me that we make sure it is. The setting of the rates of the company and the rates that we pay must not only be fair, as I said earlier, but they

must also appear to be fair. There must be no doubt about that.
I am not satisfied with the regulation of the Bell Telephone Company and particularly that the relationship between Bell and Northern is sufficiently rigid to ensure that this is the case. I do not like the interlock between these two companies. I think that at the least the accounting of Northern should be so segregated that one could see what is being charged on this outside commercial business and what is being charged on the business transacted with Bell. As a further step I should like to see, if possible, the two divisions of Northern completely segregated and divorced.
It seems to me we should do one thing if we are going to allow the present situation to continue. I think that we who have allowed this monopolistic situation to exist have a responsibility to make sure that it exists in the interests of all. I should like to see legislation passed which would cause the Bell Telephone Company to come regularly before a committee of parliament where various questions and doubts such as I have raised could be examined, and could be examined in depth.
We as parliamentarians have allowed this situation, which may be beneficial, to exist. I believe we have a responsibility as members of parliament to make sure that it exists in the best interests of all concerned. I think the company would probably welcome the opportunity to come before such a committee. There may be nothing in the doubts I have expressed. The situation may be in the best interests of all concerned. I think the company would welcome the opportunity to explain the situation and to make it clear so that people like myself would not raise these unanswered questions.

Mr. Chairman, I have strong reservations to make about this bill. In my opinion, it would be important for the government to form a committee of both houses, not only to review the charter of the company, but also to call witnesses: The private telephone companies, including the Bell Telephone Company of Canada.
As I have already said, Mr. Chairman, the Bell Telephone Company of Canada is, among companies of this type, the most powerful in the world. About 65 per cent of the equipment intended for this company is bought from the Northern Electric, which company is itself controlled by the Bell Telephone Company of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I have here the names of ten directors of Northern Electric Company. I note that the president of Northern Electric is at the same time director of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada.
Mr. Johnson, director of Northern Electric, is at the same time director of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada; Mr. Lank Herbert, who is director of the Northern Electric, is, at the same time, director of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada; Mr. Alex Lester, director of Northern Electric, is, at the same time, vice president of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, 65 per cent of all purchases of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, as far as material is concerned, are made from its own company. It is the largest "family compact" now existing in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I have the list of directors of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. I would be very happy to have the unanimous consent of the house to table this list of directors of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada as well as of many other companies that these people control. You will see then, Mr. Chairman, the family compact that exists.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Gordon for the second reading of Bill No. C-110, to facilitate the making of loans to students, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Gauthier.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house has been studying in the last few days Bill No. C-110 dealing with loans to students.
This afternoon the hon. member for Rober-val (Mr. Gauthier) moved an amendment.
When introducing that bill, the government undoubtedly had good intentions because for us and all the people of Canada, education is a very important matter since it concerns primarily a very high percentage of our young people, the future leaders of Canada. That is why the government is introducing that bill dealing with education, to enable students to continue their studies, in short to be better prepared to face life and its needs.

On the other hand, what strikes me most, a matter to which several members have drawn my attention, is that the government is intruding in a field which has nothing to do with the federal government.
It is not the first time that we in Quebec have heard about education. A few years ago the Quebec Liberals told us that our educational system was not perfect under the previous administration and that they wanted to amend it; they then promised free education.
A few years ago we were promised free education in the province of Quebec and now the federal government is discussing student loans.
On the one hand, the Liberals promise free schooling and here in Ottawa, future students, the future elite of the province of Quebec or Canada, are allowed to go into debt.
Free schooling was said to be a sheet anchor for our young people. It is realized today that it was a real deception and a measure is now being introduced in order to grant loans to Canadian students, including those of the province of Quebec, as a solution to their problems.
But if we look at what happened in other fields, for instance, when the federal government and the provincial governments have in the past made different types of loans available to the various social classes, one finds that those loans did not produce the expected results or achieve their purpose.
For instance, we remember quite well what happened as a result of the passing of measures on agricultural loans, industrial loans, loans to small industrial enterprises; today, we find that those measures have not solved the problems faced by the farmers or the manufacturers.
As far as free education is concerned, we were told that we would have nothing to pay. Today we realize that text books are more expensive than before, that the construction of our schools costs more than ever and that our school taxes are higher than ever, that the provincial sales taxes-which are mentioned in this bill have increased as well as school deficits.
What do we see in the meantime? The parents' autonomy does not exist any more, it disappeared a long time ago. We also see that the autonomy of the school boards does not exist any more; they are almost completely under the control of the provincial government.
What do we see now? The autonomy of the province of Quebec is threatened in a field

which comes under its own and exclusive jurisdiction.
Some hon. members in this house went so far as to advocate a federal department of education. Well, if that principle of centralization is so good, why not advocate also an international department of education under the United Nations? If we want to be ridiculous, we might as well go the whole way.
Would it be possible for Canada to have the same system of education as certain member countries of the United Nations? Absolutely not, and I think all hon. members will agree with me on that point.
We do not deny the other provinces the right to have their own system of education, their own culture and their own language. In return, we want our rights to be respected in the province of Quebec. The British North America Act-forgive me, Mr. Speaker, but we are still British-respects provincial rights and that is why we, in Quebec, are against not the principle of this bill but against this intrusion of the federal government in a field which does not come under its jurisdiction but under that of the provinces.
A measure for free schooling in our province was submitted to us as a last hope, as regards the education problem. It has proven a failure. We have before us today, in Ottawa, legislation on loans to students; a few years hence, we will realize that it has not given the anticipated results.
In favour of whom do we want to get our students into debt? In favour of the banks, which are the sole and actual beneficiaries under this bill-get our students into debt in favour of the banks.
Up to now we have got everybody into debt. Where are the social classes that are not in debt?
The farmers are in debt, the workers are in debt, our industries are in debt and so are our school boards. We find that our provincial governments are in debt; we also see that our federal government is in the same situation and is getting deeper into debt to put others into debt. Everyone is in debt, and now we want our students to go into debt.
With regard to this bill, a member pointed out this afternoon, that only banks can loan money to students; no other serious and responsible organization in Canada can lend money to our students.
We had our industries incur debts in favour of the banks, we had our industrial resources encumbered in favour of our banks, and today, the intention is to involve in debt 20220-353J
Loans to Students
our future natural resources for the benefit of the banks, and no other solution is being found to the present system.
The present bill is greeted with enthusiasm. How ridiculous.
As for us, we do not want debts. Students have already too many debts, their parents nave already too many debts; what the Canadian people need is an income system. Instead of making loans available to students, as is being done at the present time, why not make available to the students, during the holiday period, jobs which would make it possible for them to earn some money during the ten or 12 weeks of the summer holidays, or at least for eight or nine weeks of work?
Why should not the federal government organize some system to make employment available to the students, making it possible for them to earn $100 a week? Then they would earn during the holiday period the equivalent of the amount of $1,000 involved in the debt we want them to get into. They could this way earn money while acquiring an education, and they could then pay for their studies. But no, today, instead of offering employment to students in order that they may pay for their studies, they are allowed to study and to run into debt and, in the meantime, we also get the country into debt.
During their schooling they could work and contribute to the wealth of Canada. During their holidays they could produce something instead of doing nothing. They could also work their way through school.
We have no other system than to push them into debt. Get into debt students, farmers, industrialists, municipalities, school boards. It sounds like the system advocated by finance companies. "Travel now, pay later"; buy today, pay later; buy your house today; pay later; buy your farm today, pay later; buy your furniture today, pay later. "Consolidate your debts, re-finance them and pay later". In Bill No. C-110, our young people are being told: "study now and pay later."
Students are not begging for charity or privileges. Why not offer them jobs, giving them an opportunity to work during their holidays, instead of offering them as the only solution, debts and a mortgaged future.
Mr. Speaker, what amazes me most, is that when the problem is to develop Canada or give Canadians or our students a few amenities in peacetime, there is no money; we

Loans to Students
get debts and obligations; we have unemployment and insecurity. But come war or war preparation, everything becomes available. Why not make the same benefits available to our students.
I have here a pamphlet dealing with Canadian military colleges. Here is what it says concerning the military training of our youth. It is a lot more interesting than Bill No. C-110 I would even suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) to get acquainted with that pamphlet designed for the army, air force and navy trainees, and to redraft his bill accordingly. First, the large headline:
Enthralling life for young Canadians.
It is a lot more enthralling than what is offered our youth. It is so enthralling to enroll in the air force. Here is what is says.
1.	First class aeronautical training.
2.	Very good pay.
Not a word about debts. They are paid; there is no signing of promissory notes.
3.	Opportunity to increase your knowledge through numerous courses offered by the air force.
It is all about air force; there is no mention
of interest.
4.	Opportunity to travel in Canada and abroad.
5.	Thirty days annual leave with pay.
6! Free medical and dental care.
It is free, Mr. Minister.
7.	Work with a team sharing the same ideal.
This is interesting.
8.	Security ensured by generous retirement plans.
There is no mention of debts. Nothing is
said of a debt plan. And that is not all.
9.	Attractive and comfortable rooms for single people.
Nothing is said of married people.
10.	Organized recreation for everyone.
11.	Agreeable working conditions.
12.	Training for administrative and executive duties.
And that is not all they offer our youth headed for the air force, the army or the navy. But it is much better than what is offered by Bill No. C-110. Further, it says:
General courses leading to a diploma in arts, science and engineering are supplemented by military instruction and studies, including summer training in Canada or abroad. Tuition fees are paid by the government and cadet officers are also supplied with the required uniforms and receive pay and allowances, besides being entitled to annual leave and other privileges.
Here, one finds the amount of pay given to young students of the air force, army and navy, not for peace but for war:

Pay (aU cadet officers), $63 a month.
Living allowance, $65 a month.
And if the student does flying time:
$75 a month.
The above figures do not comprise medical and dental care, which are free, nor clothing or other benefits. The cadet officers have 30 days of annual leave with pay (to which travelling time is added), which is generally awarded after the summer training period. Christmas leave is also provided.
I wanted to point out the merits of a military educational system with regard to the air force, the army and the navy.
What a difference from the terms of Bill No. C-110, which is offered to all our young people in Canada. All we have to offer are debts and loans.
When shall we rid ourselves of that system?
I listened to hon. members, whether Conservative or Liberal, and I found that whenever there was a question of taxes or loans, they were all in agreement.
Mr. Speaker, the weather is upon us; each summer, the flies appear with the heat. What do the farmers do? They get an insect killer, which is called d.d.t., to kill those flies.
As far as I am concerned, I say that the two old line parties represented in this chamber, the Liberals and the Conservatives, use exactly the same remedies, the same pattern to destroy our social classes: the d.d.t. system. In fact, since confederation, Canada never has had anything else than debts, deficits and taxes. That is, sirs, your d.d.t. financial system. Today, there is nothing else to offer our various social classes.
This afternoon the hon. member for Rob-erval proposed an amendment to the bill under consideration. Why? To allow students to achieve the same results, without incurring debts and mortgaging their future as their parents are presently doing.
We want the federal government to respect the British North America Act. The separatist movement in the province of Quebec is criticized, the French Canadians who want to safeguard the province's autonomy are blamed. But the federal ministers should start by respecting the British North America Act, which gave the provinces jurisdiction over education, instead of interfering in a field which comes under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces.
The amendment moved by the hon. member for Roberval would enable the Bank of Canada to loan the provinces, without interest,

the money they need to do what they want in the field of education.
The British North America Act gave the provinces jurisdiction in the field of education but, on the other hand, jurisdiction in the field of finance was given to the federal government. The provinces were entrusted with responsibility in the field of education, but the means to carry out that responsibility were given to the central government.
Now, since finance and money come under the federal government and since education is a provincial responsibility, Ottawa should, through the Bank of Canada, put the required funds at the disposal of the provinces, so that the latter may look after educational needs as they see fit. If that were the case, we would hear less about separatism because provincial and minority rights would be respected. It is only on that condition that the Canadian confederation will be strong; otherwise, we will inevitably end up on the road on which Bill No. C-110 is but a milestone.
This separatism wave will unfortunately get worse in Quebec, not because of the separatists themselves, but because of those who are sitting on the government benches. [Text]
Mr. L. T. Pennell (Parliamentary Secretary
to Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, my intervention will unfortunately be technical in nature but, fortunately, brief in character. The time has come when I feel that some observations ought to be made on the very difficult constitutional and legal aspects of the debate before the house. But before I do so may I be allowed to interpose a welcome to the principles of the bill. There is a rule that says that something is always lost in translation, but it seems to me that the very instructive and illuminating introductory explanation by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) proved to be the exception to the rule.
I confidently believe that any measure which has as its fundamental purpose to widen the opportunities for education will receive a sympathetic treatment at the hands of this house. Its aim is to wipe out the inequalities imposed by economic handicaps.
It may interest the house to know that in the recent report of the Robbins commission in Great Britain they found that they had to change their views regarding the relationship between heredity and intelligence. They found that the children of the lower class people did just as well as children of upper and middle class groups. May I suggest that a great
Loans to Students
resource of untapped ability in this nation will be found in the working class and lower income groups. I speak with some experience, Mr. Speaker, and, with deep feeling on this matter when I say that no young persons should have to be deprived of, or delayed the opportunity for, education at a university, and it is bitter tea to swallow when you have to undergo that experience. It is a trite observation to say that this nation must make the fullest possible use of its capital resources and in intelligence.
I now pass by natural transition to the
very difficult constitutional points that probe deeply into the fabric of this bill. I know that a large number of the members of this house are not lawyers, and I suppose they will thank me for that testimonial. But none the less I believe there is a legitimate curiosity about these very fundamental legal problems.
I turn at once to deal in particular with the criticism contained in the speech of the hon. and learned member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), to which the house listened with unbroken attention. If I understood him correctly, and I think I did, his argument was put in this way. He stated that the purport of this bill was to delegate the power of the parliament of Canada, a sovereign authority, to the lieutenant governor in council, who in turn would make a very important decision by designating persons or agencies who would select the student as qualifying and the institutions designated under the act.
The hon. and learned member went on to draw our attention to the case of the attorney general of Nova Scotia v. attorney general of Canada, which is reported in Supreme Court Reports, 1951. That case held that it was unconstitutional for the parliament of Canada to delegate its power to a provincial legislature.
It should be noted Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member then made a distinction and pointed out that the Nova Scotia case was different from the case now engaging the attention of the house because in the Nova Scotia case the delegation of power was from the parliament of Canada to the provincial legislature, while the purport of this bill delegates power from parliament to the lieutenant governor in council.
I do not think I do an injustice to the very forceful argument of the hon. member for Greenwood when I say that he did not cite any case that turned directly on the point, so far as the lieutenant governor in council

Loans to Students
is concerned. He bridged that difference, may I say, by stating that in his opinion the principle was applicable in both cases. It is at this point that I must part company, with great reluctance, from the hon. member. I might say that the answer to his argument is found in his own distinction. The bill now before the house is a delegation not from the parliament of Canada to the provincial legislature, but a delegation from parliament to the lieutenant governor in council. In any event-and this is a fundamental point-the bill does not purport to delegate any legislative authority but only delegate administrative authority, which the lieutenant governor in council can carry out without the consent of the provincial legislature.
May I put it another way, Mr. Speaker. The bill is not purporting to take any lawmaking powers away from the parliament of Canada to give to the lieutenant governor in council, because the parliament of Canada has already exercised its law-making powers which are contained in the bill itself. All we are doing is permitting the lieutenant governor in council to make an administrative act which, as I say, in no way affects the law-making power which remains with parliament.
Perhaps I may be allowed to cite an illustration in support of the contention I now put forward. If the house would bear with me I should like to invite its attention to the Canadian World Exhibition Corporation Act, section 10, which act is to be found in Statutes of Canada, 1962-63, chapter 12. Section 10 says, quoting the material words:
The corporation shall.. .submit for the approval of the governor in council and the lieutenant governor in council its over-all plan-
This is an illustration of the parliament of Canada delegating authority to the lieutenant governor in council to approve a certain plan. May I say-I do not say this in any arrogant or offensive manner-that in this case the lieutenant governor in council was that of the province of Quebec. Without trying to make a political point, Mr. Speaker, being secure in the knowledge that a large number of members across the floor of the house will support the bill, may I say that perhaps they will secure further comfort from the knowledge that the legislation to which I have just referred was introduced, and properly introduced, by the previous administration.
But my illustrations do not stop there. I would ask the house to apply its mind to the Criminal Code, sections 523, 524, 526 and

527, in all of which sections, power of the parliament was delegated to the lieutenant governor in council to carry out administrative acts regarding people declared insane and held in detention.
I could, Mr. Speaker, refer to section 13 of the Prisons and Reformatories Act, which deals with powers conferred by parliament on the lieutenant governor to make regulations to prevent escape from jail. Section 20 of the Juvenile Delinquents Act deals with powers conferred by parliament on the lieutenant governor in council to approve an industrial school to which children who are judged to be juvenile delinquents may be committed.
I do not wish to pretend by the fact that I have cited a number of similar illustrations that I have entirely removed the arguments of my hon. friend from Greenwood. I have a profound respect for him. I knew him at the bar and his reputation preceded him into this house. Whenever he makes an assertion on constitutional law it ought to be listened to with attention. But may I also say that those of us who are concerned with the bill have made an honest and sincere effort to see that it stays within proper limits. We have given sustained consideration to the matter and I would ask the house, particularly the hon. member for Greenwood, to whom I make a personal appeal although he is not present, to accept the opinion that the bill does not contravene and is within the rule of constitutional purity and substance.
I should not ignore the fact that the learned member proposed an alternative method and in my very humble opinion that alternative was valid and did not affect the fabric of the bill. But I am sure he will understand our position. We have given this matter a great deal of attention, have turned it over in our minds a great number of times, and we have reached the conscientious and honest opinion that the bill does not in any way infringe on the rights of the provinces, or is unconstitutional.

Under the leading case of Tenant v. Union Bank of Canada, 1894 Appeal Cases, 31, a privy council decision, it was laid down that "banking is an expression wide enough to embrace every transaction coming within the legitimate business of a banker".
I say it is within the concept of banking to make loans, and if the bank makes loans surely it should have the right to recover the money due to it. Forgetting the question of law altogether, in my respectful submission it would be contrary to common sense to call something a loan if the man who paid out the money did not have the right to attempt to recover.
Therefore I submit that this question of loans properly comes under the category of banking as defined in section 91 (15) of the B.N.A. Act. I would also direct the attention of the house to the leading case of attorney general of Canada v. attorney general of Quebec, a 1947 judgment, also by the privy council, in which it was held that a depositor had a right to recover his deposit from the bank and that this was a matter of

banking and not a contractual matter relating to property and civil rights. I notice that the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) shakes his head, but all I can do is give the authority. The privy council decision in the case of attorney general of Canada and attorney general of Quebec.

The bank may.. .without the authority, aid, assistance or intervention of any other person or official being required,
(a)	receive deposits from any person whomsoever, whatever his age, status or condition in life, and whether such person is qualified by law to enter into ordinary contracts or not.
This section implies a right in the depositor to claim payment from the bank and it sets up a bank-customer relationship in which each party has equal rights. Therefore I submit that clause 15 is properly included as a part of banking.

I am

I am also one of those who believe that this legislation has been brought forward much too late. I regret that some of the statements made during the course of this debate have been somewhat contrary to what has actually happened during the course of this parliament. I should like to say initially, Mr. Speaker, that the point that aroused my interest in the bill was the intervention on July 14 of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso). I asked the hon. member a question at the conclusion of his remarks, and I should like to repeat a portion of that question in order to clarify my position this evening. I quote from page 5477 of Hansard:
Will the hon. member permit a question? Does he not agree that had it not been for the efforts of the Canadian students union itself, goodness knows when we would have had this legislation?
I shall not quote the other portion of the question because that is the important part. The hon. member for Hamilton West said he was happy I had asked him the question. Then, he said:
He should look at the position of his own side. He says, now: We are willing to co-operate: put the legislation before us. But it is interesting to note that the opposition has only adopted this attitude after pressure by the students, by he universities and in the press.
In my opinion, this is an extremely important inference. My predecessor on the floor this evening said he was making his contribution on a non-political basis, and 1 made it very clear at that time my presentation to the government, in order to impress them with the importance of this legislation, had been on a non-political basis as well. I assure you this evening that was the case, and it remains so this evening.
I should like to refer to some of the remarks made earlier in the debate by the same hon. member for Hamilton West. At page 5474 of Hansard he refers to the words of Mr. James G. Mitchell, president of the students council of the University of Waterloo and James D. Kraemer, chairman of the board of external relations of that university.

This is what those men said in a letter to the hon. member:
The Ontario legislature did not adequately meet the needs of her expanding universities and as a result there has been a widespread increase in tuition fees (a situation common throughout Canada). The increase in fees (which in our case amounts to more than $75) coupled with the growing scarcity of summer employment once again threatened to make "university" a "privilege of the wealthy".
Earlier in their letter they say:
Our earnest hope is that the members of parliament will effectively expedite this priority legislation-

-which awaits the house, in order that a system of federal loans for students will be in effect for September, 1964.
How ridiculous can a person be? I watched the activities of the hon. member for Hamilton West very carefully. I regret very much that he is not in the house this evening, nor has he been in the house all day today, nor was he at the meeting of university students held in room 112 north in this building when they made their presentation, nor do I find one instance of the hon. member putting that presentation before the government or requesting that this legislation be brought forward. This angers me more than a little, because he accused the opposition of not intervening until the Canadian students union made a presentation to the government.

That is right, Stanley. Then on page 5139, July 7, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre again, and on page 5150, July 7, which happens to be myself, Mr. Speaker, and I will stop there; but there were other requests.
Let it not be said by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso) that we boarded the gravy train when the Canadian students union arrived. I am afraid the government did not become alive to the situation until that date.
Again my predecessor in speaking, the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Pennell), said that he was a learned member of the law profession and might be in a minority in this house. Sometimes I think there are too many of them here, Mr. Speaker, but I still tell you I have a very high regard for that member, and regardless of the constitutional arguments or involvements I am prepared to support every inch of this legislation, including the resultant problems that will be created.
When I say the resultant problems I refer to some of the references that have been made. I think of facility; I think of faculty as well as of the student. It does not matter too much to me in which order we take them. If this legislation creates the next problem, then I say well and good, because if there is one thing we need in this country right now it is a look at the educational system to improve it and to create greater opportunity.
It is a peculiar thing, when we look at the expenditures of the government and the manner in which they are made, the first thing supporters of the government say is, what did you do when your government was in office? That kind of thinking in this particular case, as in others, must be forgotten and I say to you, Mr. Speaker, if we look into the future we have to think of the tax dollars we are going to spend.
In this connection I am thinking of the unemployment insurance fund and am suggesting that we take a look at the drop-outs in secondary school and high school. Maybe

we can do something in this area because to my way of thinking there is no sense in educating students through grades 11 and 12, particularly in the province of Ontario, and have them drop out only to see a diminishing supply of money in the unemployment insurance fund. That is poor business. We should think far enough on into the future about the way we are going to spend our tax dollars, and maybe we shall have to revise our entire thinking.
I think of the whiz kids the Minister of Finance brought in to assist him with his first budget. Maybe three or four of those unemployed people could have spent that money much more realistically than the whiz kids spent it. When you draw the common denominator of people who apply for unemployment insurance, as the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand has said, if we use the thinking power of these people we will be able to understand better their problems. All the brains of the country are not in parliament. As a matter of fact, it was not too long ago I thought most of the brains were outside parliament; but when we consider where the money is going to be best spent we should have a look at the whole picture.
Maybe we should bring in some of the presidents of our universities so that we can more readily understand exactly what the requirements are. Even though we have very valuable and high minded contributions during the course of this debate we will not find the solution to all the problems that exist. One criticism of this legislation which I heard was that put forward by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam in regard to the bank loan situation that has existed thus far concerning students.
It just so happens that this afternoon I had the president of the Waterloo Lutheran University in my office and he discussed this with me. He assured me that never once did they have a problem with a student who had a reasonable standing, in securing a loan. I asked him, "Will this legislation serve a very useful purpose in your institution?" and his reply was, "Yes, to a degree it will assist us in that our own bursary program will not have to be so great."
Without offering it as a vital criticism of this legislation, the question is, why was it not brought forward as it was promised? I do not ask this to indicate that I am opposed to it. I am not, as I have said; but when the Liberal party promises scholarships in an election campaign and turns around and converts them into a loan program, surely to

goodness the people of Canada will wake up and have a look at what they are doing with the country and how they are putting their program forward. Is it truthful? I am not saying it is untruthful, but I ask you, Mr. Speaker, and members of the house, is it truthful if you are going to give scholarships and you turn around and make them loans?
The president of this university said to me this afternoon the one thing they were always careful of was the debt position into which a student placed himself. I replied, "Surely, when a student is going on for a professional career a debt of $3,000 or $4,000 is not too much to him". He replied that there are so many complications for a student going through university today. Some come in as married people; some of them are married immediately they graduate. "Now," he said, "it may be a minority of the group, but it creates a situation which must be looked at responsibly."
I have had some of the members of this house say to me that the provincial programs are inadequate. I do not know whether I am prepared to say they are inadequate. I have here before me the program as outlined by the department of education of the province of Ontario entitled "Ontario Student Aid Loans, 1964-65." It is a complete outline of that program. I am not prepared to read it out fully and put it on the record, but it does not look too bad to me in relation to what the president of this university had to say to me today. It does give the student who is eligible, who has the desire, and has the capability, the opportunity of going further along, with the money he might borrow from a chartered bank.
Contrary to what the hon. member for Hamilton West had to say, I deny that everything is political expediency. He seems to think no one has his eyes open until such time as legislation is brought forward or some pressure group comes into the picture. There is another thing I should like to point out in this regard. It was very interesting to me to note what happened the day we met the students union. I did not identify myself by name or by party and I stated at that meeting that my contribution, or questions, or presentation was on a non-political basis, whereupon all the Liberal members immediately howled me down. Of course we know what this is: It is the usual practice. But I think, now that the situation is somewhat different, and even at the cost of that trifling and usual Liberal embarrassment I stand here and say 20220-354J

I intend to support this legislation; I think it is good and I hope it goes through at the earliest possible date.
Some time ago, as I was about to say to you, Mr. Speaker, early in May, being concerned that the legislation was not coming forward quickly enough-and I hope the excerpts I read to you and the house are sufficient to prove that at least we were sincere in what we were doing-I wrote to the minister of education in the province of Ontario, and he had this to say to me:
You will notice that loans of $500 are available to Ontario residents taking courses in the institutions as listed for the current year. The appropriation for this fund is $3 million and we anticipate that all of it will be used.
Therefore I suggest again to the house that this is a valuable piece of legislation and I hope it is consummated in time for all the students who require it to make use of it.
With regard now to the student who puts himself in a debt position, I should like to say that I have before me a prospectus for the United States economy as put forward by a firm known as Vince, Saunders and Company, Inc., of Boston, Massachusetts. It is interesting to note that these statistics, which are dated June 15, 1964, indicate that by 1975 the gross national product of the United States will increase by more than 50 per cent to a record of $1 trillion per year. It is also estimated that there will be an increase of 40 per cent in today's average income and that the average family income in the United States will be $8,724 by 1975. There are a number of other statistics which I shall not bother to place on record, but I believe that this, together with the other quotations I have given, indicates that we must proceed, and proceed quickly in the direction we are now taking.
We all know, and it has been stated in the course of this debate, what the government has contributed to the universities on a per capita basis, and I hope-I do not know whether this has been mentioned; if not, I put it forward for what it is worth-that these contributions are made on a per capita basis of the student population of the universities rather than on the basis of the populations of the provinces of Canada concerned.
Some institutions are of course more progressive than others. We heard yesterday and last evening of the tremendous growth which will be experienced here in the capital city and I am sure a similar growth, if not a greater growth, will take place in the industrial centres of this country such as Mont-

Loans to Students
real, Toronto, and so on. These areas surely can no longer be segregated on a provincial basis. In such cases, let us relate our contribution directly to the institution so as to enable them to do the job with which they have been entrusted. Let us not restrict them in any way. This would take care of universities in the maritime area where, as I understand it from the debate, they have a tremendous number of students attending from other parts of Canada. Then the other provinces can take advantage accordingly, and in this way there will be the proper distribution of the funds which are necessary.
I listened with great interest to some of the high minded speeches which have come from the government side of the house. I hesitate to say this again, because one becomes tarnished with a political approach in this house and outside. This is used for the purpose of showing something other than the sincerity with which a point is put forward. This evening I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house, that some time ago I was involved in the possibility of the opening of a university at the Edgar radar site in Ontario, half way between Orillia and Barrie. I was intimately concerned with the progress of this particular proposal. The government came forward with suggestions. Members were working. Defeated candidates were working-and that is the important part of the question. Then all of a sudden there was a change. The government was not so vitally interested. They are now. And who pulled the rug from under the government? Their own defeated Liberal members. Yes, that is quite so.
I understand, some time in the future there is to be a university at Barrie, and I congratulate the people who are to take part in the establishment of that university. But if the government had had their sights set precisely in the first instance there would be an institution of learning at Edgar and maybe some time in the future they will regret not having established it. Let us not be so high minded about a piece of legislation here in the house in one instance and then play around with politics outside as seems to be a characteristic of this government-and it is regrettable that it must occur.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to say a few

words in support of this bill and in opposition of the amendment to it. I think that the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler), before criticizing in any way the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso), should spend some time correcting his own colleagues who feel that this bill is unconstitutional and who do not seem prepared to support it. I say this in a rather non-political sense-I hope, in a more non-political sense than the hon. member-because I am quite pleased to note that he himself supports this legislation. If he wants to find very good authority from a leader of his own party on the attitude to take toward this matter, I have a quotation for him which reads as follows:
The challenge of adventure into new fields of social welfare must not find us discouraged by the difficulties adherent in the British North America Act. We must go forth into new horizons of social justice.. .The state must guarantee and underwrite equal access to security, to education, to nutrition and to health for all.
These words were spoken by the then member for Lake Centre, the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) during the debate on the family allowance bill in 1944, and can be found in volume VI of Hansard for that year at page 5460. I hope, therefore, the members of the official opposition who support this bill will bring this quotation to the attention of their colleagues who do not seem to share their views.
The University of Windsor, the Windsor teachers' college and the western Ontario institute of technology are all found in the riding of Essex West, and of course this helps indicate the basis for my interest in this bill.
The University of Windsor in the last few years has had a spectacular growth and development, much of which has come about under the inspired leadership of the Reverend Father E. C. Lebel. Father Lebel recently retired as president of the University of Windsor but will be continuing his work in the field of higher education as principal of St. Mark's college of the University of British Columbia. I know I speak for all the people of Windsor in adding further words of tribute to the many already expressed for his splendid service to the university and our community. The period of Father Lebel's work in Windsor reflects what has happened to higher education in Canada over the past several decades. When he came to Assumption college, a precursor of the university in 1941, to head its English department, three buildings were sufficient to provide both for housing and classrooms for some 100 college students and those of an affiliated high school. When he
Loans to Students
completed his last days as president at the end of June of this year the University of Windsor had grown to include some 11 buildings and some 3,965 students of which 1,816 were full time.
Yet the University of Windsor and the other universities in our country still have much to do to meet the demands that are being placed upon them. We are privileged in Windsor to have as Father Lebel's successor Dr. John Francis Leddy, former vice president of the University of Saskatchewan. Jerry Hames of the Windsor Star recently interviewed Dr. Leddy, and in a report in the Windsor Star of July 3, 1964, said that Dr. Leddy "showed concern for the large numbers of students who have attained university entrance standards, yet find themselves through either lack of accommodation or financial need unable to enrol in university".
Mr. Hames went on to quote Dr. Leddy as saying "there are more capable students who find themselves outside university than those who are actually enrolled in the university courses throughout Canada. It weighs very heavily upon me". Mr. Speaker, this is a matter that should weigh very heavily upon all Canadians, not only because of the injustice this situation has meant to the individuals concerned who up till now have not been able to obtain the higher education of which they are capable, but also because of the loss it has meant to our country of badly needed skills. I know that the majority of Canadians in all parts of our country will therefore welcome this legislation, which I think will do much to deal with the problem of financial need that has kept many young people from our universities and other institutions of higher learning.
I must say that in presenting this important legislation-and I say this in the same non-partisan, non-political sense as the hon. member for Grey-Bruce-within only a year and several months after taking office, this government has done something which the previous Conservative government was unable to do in six years of office, during four of which they had the biggest majority in Canadian history.
I think we should again take the opportunity to make absolutely clear that at least as far as I am aware this Canada student loan plan is definitely not being put forward in substitution for or in place of the 10,000 scholarships program which formed part of the platform on which we campaigned and gained office in 1963.

speechtext:
Where are they?

Loans to Students

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
I might add, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Hamilton West has no need to stand in this house during the question period or otherwise to avow his support of this program, because it formed part of the program on which he went to the people of his riding and in which he defeated a former Conservative cabinet minister.
The student loan fund and the university scholarships program were both part of our program for creating greater opportunities for our youth, of which the extension of family allowances formed another important part. We have already implemented one such program, the youth allowances, which I am very happy to support and which has the effect of extending the family allowance program. In presenting to parliament this measure with regard to student loans we are now proceeding with a further stage and I am personally confident that this government will seek an early and appropriate opportunity to present to parliament the program for the 10,000 scholarships as a further stage of our program for creating greater opportunity for our youth.
Opposition speakers have suggested that the making available of student loans will increase the strain on the capacity of our universities. However, it should not be forgotten that a study published in February of this year by the Canadian universities foundation stated, "In spite of a general continued increase in university enrolment, the situation in the fall of 1963 shows that there are still places in university for those who meet the minimum requirements". Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in spite of the obvious desperate need for more buildings there is room at this time for those who can take advantage of this student loan fund.
Every once in a while we still hear people say that any student who wants to go out and do so can earn all the money needed for tuition fees, room and board and other expenses. Research shows that this is simply not the case. According to the recent Canadian union of students-Loyola university-survey on student summer employment, 82 per cent of students work in the summer months but only slightly more than 50 per cent earn between $300 and $1,000; yet the average undergraduate costs run between $1,196 and $1,550.
The possibility of students being able to earn the money needed for their education from part time work is getting smaller and smaller. Many of the part time, summer jobs available to students at one time simply do

not exist any more due to changes in technology. It is also clear that existing bursary and scholarship programs available through the provinces or through private sources are simply not sufficient to meet the need. If this were not so, Mr. Speaker, over half of those capable of higher education would not be outside our universities. This is further demonstrated by an interesting table showing student retention from secondary school to university which is to be found in the 1963-64 Canada Year Book. This table shows that of those entering grade 2 only about 15 per cent enter the senior school leaving year, and about 9 per cent enter university. And of those, only about 5 per cent graduate from university with a first degree.
For anyone to talk at this time, for example, of tightening admission standards to hold down the number of those seeking entrance to university is to urge a cruel and unrealistic solution and one which is dangerous to the future of this country. This country has so great a need for the skills which can come from higher education that it simply cannot afford to permit anyone capable of benefiting from higher education to be deprived of it for financial reasons. Canada can no longer leave the filling of this need largely to chance in the manner followed up to now-the chance which gave a student prosperous parents, or which brought him a good summer or part time job, or even the chance which gave him the stamina to follow his studies and to work at the same time.
Conditions in the world and in this country now are such that it is as much in the interests of the Canadian community to enable the young person to obtain a university education as it was, and still is, to provide him with a primary and secondary education. About 100 years ago systems of primary and secondary education available to all and supported by the community were created because they benefited the entire community. Secondary education and even primary education at that time was sufficient to enable most of the people to fill most of the jobs available and to carry out their duties as citizens. But today our world has changed to such a degree that merely to meet the same requirements of having a population able to carry out needed tasks and duties as citizens, the community must also be willing to assume the cost of making available higher education. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there is no logical reason today why the community through one of its governmental manifestations or another should

pay the cost of primary and secondary schooling but stay away from university training and education at a similar level.
We have to eliminate the idea that still lingers that in providing aid to those seeking university training we are bestowing some type of favour mainly for the private benefit of the student. It is true that university graduates earn higher incomes, but these incomes arising out of the greater productivity which is brought about by their higher degree of skill will not only benefit the community but will enable us to bear the cost not only of comprehensive social welfare programs but also the aid to higher education itself.
Most important of all, measures of the nature of the student loan fund will help make sure that Canada has the skills it must have to move ahead in today's highly competitive trading world. Without these skills our products will not be able to compete with those of other nations with ever-advancing technology. The maintenance and development of our standard of living depends on this parliament passing measures of the type we are debating. We must look upon the cost of this student loan fund and other measures which will follow as a form of investment in what is surely our most valuable resource-our young people, and the return on this investment will far exceed the expense.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, this student loan fund is not of itself the complete answer to the needs involved in paying the cost of higher education both to the competent student and to the university he attends. But it is a significant and an important step forward toward the goal of ensuring that no one who has the desire and the ability will be deprived of higher education for financial reasons in Canada. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, to paraphrase the words of Dr. Leddy, president of the University of Windsor, this problem must continue to weigh heavily upon all of us until this vital goal is reached.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like first of all to congratulate the minister upon bringing in this legislation, timid though it is. I wonder what happened, however, to those 10,000 scholarships.

speechtext: Just wait.
